meta.description: Universal title-craft library: structural title formulas and scoring rules derived from what makes any YouTube title click — curiosity gap, specificity, length discipline, honest framing. Niche-agnostic; the channel's niche and audience fill in the subject.

thumbnail_system.name: Short Thumbnail Line
rules: Keep it to 2-4 words. Shorter is stronger.
No YOUR or YOU language — ever.
It should amplify the concept, not repeat the full title.
Think: the single punchiest phrase that captures the moment.
Bold, high-contrast text (heavy weight, outline, or backing) so it reads at small size.
Must be readable at mobile thumbnail size (160x90px).
bad_examples: YOUR LIFE CHANGES FOREVER (too long, uses YOUR)
THIS WILL SHOCK YOU (vague hype, uses YOU)
YOU WON'T BELIEVE THIS (uses YOU, empty hype)
EVERYTHING ABOUT THE TOPIC (too long, vague)

title_thumbnail_pairing.rule: Title and thumbnail line should cover different parts of the curiosity gap. The title carries the specific 'what' and 'who'. The thumbnail line is a short 2-4 word punch — it amplifies, it does not repeat the title.

examples.title: How One Cook Fixed the Hardest Sauce in French Cuisine
Why Most English Learners Stall at the Same Point
The Small Habit That Changed How She Studies

master_formulas.name: Direct Mechanism (Search-First)
master_formulas.psychology: Maximum clarity. Tells the viewer exactly what they'll learn. Optimized for YouTube Search ranking. No cleverness needed — the subject is inherently interesting.
master_formulas.best_for: Clear how-it-works explainers, breaking/recent events, step-by-step mechanisms
examples: How One Cook Fixed the Hardest Sauce in French Cuisine
How a Small Studio Built a Hit Game in Six Months
How This Method Doubles Reading Speed

master_formulas.name: Hidden Mechanism
master_formulas.psychology: Names a subject + implies something not widely known + a specific 'how' creates an irresistible curiosity gap.
master_formulas.best_for: Behind-the-scenes mechanisms, surprising methods, things hidden in plain sight
examples: How Top Chefs Quietly Speed Up Prep
How This App Actually Keeps You Hooked
How One Teacher Really Gets Kids Reading

master_formulas.name: Causal Authority ('Why' Opener)
master_formulas.psychology: Promises a causal explanation, not just facts. The viewer will UNDERSTAND something, not merely hear about it.
master_formulas.best_for: Cause-and-effect explainers, structural problems, 'why does this happen' questions
examples: Why Most English Learners Stall at the Same Point
Why This Recipe Never Works the First Time
Why Indie Games Keep Outselling the Big Studios

master_formulas.name: Vague Signal + Specific Subject
master_formulas.psychology: Maximum curiosity from the vagueness of 'something', grounded by the specificity of a real subject.
master_formulas.best_for: Emerging shifts, surprising trends, paradigm changes in a known area
examples: Something Strange Is Happening with Home Baking
Something Changed in How We Learn Languages
Something Unexpected Is Happening in Indie Music

master_formulas.name: Superlative Deep-Dive
master_formulas.psychology: Mini-movie title-card effect. A superlative signals definitive, deep-dive content worth the watch.
master_formulas.best_for: Definitive deep dives, record stories, the-most-X-in-its-field pieces
examples: Sourdough — The Hardest Bread to Get Right
The Greatest Comeback in Indie Game History
The Most Useful Trick in Spoken English

master_formulas.name: More Than You Thought
master_formulas.psychology: Implies the viewer's current understanding is incomplete and invites them to close the gap.
master_formulas.best_for: Reframing something the viewer already knows about, myth-busting, hidden depth
examples: Espresso Is Harder Than You Think
Grammar Matters Less Than You Think
This Old Game Is Deeper Than Anyone Realizes

master_formulas.name: Possessive Shift
master_formulas.psychology: Compact and authoritative. The possessive signals deep-dive specificity; the adjective adds an emotional dimension.
master_formulas.best_for: Slow-burn change stories, profiles, the gradual rise or decline of a subject
examples: Bread's Quiet Comeback
One Channel's Surprising Turnaround
A Language App's Slow Decline

master_formulas.name: Parenthetical Stakes Escalation
master_formulas.psychology: The main clause hooks; the parenthetical escalates the stakes or adds a surprising twist.
master_formulas.best_for: Stories with a cascading consequence or a twist worth teasing
examples: This Recipe is Everywhere (and most people make it wrong)
The Game is Free (and that's the whole strategy)
Fluency is Closer Than It Feels (and here's the proof)

legacy_formulas.note: Reserved for channel-specific or legacy title shapes. LEGACY ONLY — do not use as primary generation formulas. Kept for backward compatibility and edge cases. Currently empty; the universal master_formulas above are the source of truth.

scoring_rules.description: Score each title candidate 0-100 using these weighted criteria. The criteria are universal title craft; the niche decides which subjects and framing fit.

criteria.name: specific_subject_present
criteria.rule: Title MUST name a specific, concrete subject (a real thing, person, place, dish, method, number — not a vague category). A vague subject ('stuff', 'things', 'the topic') scores 0 here.
criteria.rationale: Specificity of subject is the strongest predictor of clicks across niches. Vague subjects underperform everywhere.

criteria.name: emotional_stakes_clear
criteria.rule: The stakes or payoff must be obvious within the first 50 characters — what the viewer gains, avoids, or finally understands. Match the emotional register to the niche.
criteria.rationale: Titles that telegraph a clear payoff outperform those that merely describe a topic.

criteria.name: curiosity_gap_calibrated
criteria.rule: The title promises something specific the viewer doesn't yet know but wants to. The gap must sit between what the viewer currently knows and what the title promises.
criteria.rationale: Too vague = no click. Too complete = no need to click. The gap must be answerable but surprising.

criteria.name: front_loaded_hook
criteria.rule: The primary subject and the emotional hook must appear in the first 50 characters (the mobile truncation point).
criteria.rationale: Mobile truncation occurs at 45-50 characters. The hook must survive truncation.

criteria.name: niche_appropriate_framing
criteria.rule: The framing fits what the channel's niche actually rewards. As a general principle a sharper emotional frame (tension, stakes, a surprising turn) tends to out-click a flat one, but do NOT force crisis/threat language onto a niche that doesn't want it.
criteria.rationale: Framing that out-clicks is real, but the right frame is niche-dependent — desire for cooking, clarity for learning, stakes for investigations.

hard_rules: Total length: 30-55 characters. HARD CEILING of 55 characters. Under 45 is ideal. Mobile truncation occurs at 45-50 characters — the most compelling part of the title must be visible on mobile.

NEVER use second-person 'YOU/YOUR' language in titles. No commands ('NEVER do...', 'STOP doing...'). No imperatives. Titles are declarative statements or 'How/Why' framings about the subject, not instructions to the viewer.
NEVER use ALL CAPS words in titles except genuine acronyms. No 'NEVER', 'STOP', 'ACTUALLY' in caps. These signal clickbait and reduce CTR.
No question marks unless the question is genuinely unanswered. Declarative titles generally outperform questions.
ALWAYS name a specific, concrete subject — no vague categories.
Front-load the hook: the most compelling word and the specific subject should appear early, before truncation.
Use numbers or concrete details when available — they add specificity and tend to lift CTR.
Thumbnail line must be DIFFERENT from the title — a short 2-4 word punch, not a repeat.
